tagline: The story of Jesus the Messiah, son of David and son of Abraham, told for readers steeped in Israel's Scriptures, from his birth to his command to make disciples of all nations.
overview:
Matthew is the first book of the New Testament and the Gospel the early church quoted most. A Gospel (from an old English word for good news) is an account of the life, teaching, death, and resurrection of Jesus. Matthew tells that story with Israel's Scriptures always in view. It opens with a genealogy tracing Jesus back through King David to Abraham, and it repeatedly pauses to say that something happened to fulfill what the Lord had spoken through the prophet. Its Jesus is the promised Messiah (in Greek, Christ, the anointed king), the teacher greater than Moses, and Immanuel, God with us.

The book follows Jesus from his birth in Bethlehem under King Herod, through his baptism by John and his ministry of teaching and healing in Galilee, to his final week in Jerusalem, his crucifixion under the Roman governor Pontius Pilate, and his resurrection. Woven through the story are five long blocks of teaching, beginning with the Sermon on the Mount, which make Matthew the fullest collection of Jesus' words among the Gospels. The Gospel is also marked by conflict with the religious leaders of Jesus' day and by a widening horizon: it begins with Magi from the east worshiping the child and ends with the risen Jesus sending his disciples to all nations.

Matthew matters because it answers two questions at once. For Jewish readers it shows that Jesus is the fulfillment of Israel's hope, not a break from it. For readers from the nations it shows that the God of Israel has opened his kingdom to the whole world. It has shaped Christian prayer (the Lord's Prayer), ethics (the Beatitudes), and mission (the Great Commission) more than almost any other book.
author:
The Gospel itself is anonymous; no sentence in it names its author. The title According to Matthew appears on the earliest manuscripts that preserve a title, and the church from the second century onward attributed the book to Matthew, the tax collector whom Jesus called to follow him (9:9) and who was one of the twelve apostles (10:3). Papias, a bishop in Asia Minor in the early second century whose words are preserved by the historian Eusebius, reported that Matthew arranged the sayings of Jesus in the Hebrew language (which may mean Hebrew or Aramaic, or a Hebrew style), and Irenaeus later in the second century repeated the tradition.

Many modern scholars doubt that the apostle wrote the Greek Gospel we have. Most hold that Matthew used the Gospel of Mark as a source, reproducing much of it closely, and they think it unlikely that an eyewitness apostle would depend so heavily on the account of someone who was not. They also note that the Greek does not read like a translation from Hebrew. On this view the author was an anonymous Jewish Christian, deeply learned in the Scriptures, writing for a mostly Jewish-Christian community, and the name Matthew may have been attached because some of the material, perhaps a collection of sayings, came from him. Scholars who defend apostolic authorship answer that an apostle could reasonably use a trusted account such as Mark's, tied by tradition to Peter, that the unanimous early attribution is hard to explain if it was a guess, and that the detail about tax and money in the Gospel suits a former tax collector. Some also hold that Matthew was written first and that Mark used it, a minority view today.
date: Matthew does not state when it was written, and dates proposed range from the 50s or 60s to the 80s AD, with a few scholars going later. Those who date it before AD 70 point to passages that seem to assume the temple is still standing, such as offering a gift at the altar (5:23-24) and paying the temple tax (17:24-27), and to the early church's tradition that Matthew was the first Gospel written. Many who hold that Matthew used Mark, usually dated to the late 60s, place Matthew around AD 80 to 90. They point to the parable of the wedding banquet, where the king sends troops to burn the city (22:7), which they read as reflecting Jerusalem's destruction by Rome in AD 70, and to the Gospel's sharp distance from their synagogues, which they connect with the growing separation between church and synagogue after the war. Defenders of an earlier date reply that predicting the fall of Jerusalem needs no hindsight, since the prophets had spoken of such judgment before. Where it was written is also unknown; Antioch in Syria is the most common suggestion, with Galilee or elsewhere in Syria and Palestine also proposed.
setting:
Jesus was born near the end of the reign of Herod the Great, the king whom Rome appointed over Judea and who ruled from 37 to 4 BC. After Herod's death his kingdom was divided among his sons: Archelaus received Judea and Samaria until Rome removed him in AD 6 and placed Judea under Roman governors (Pontius Pilate governed from about AD 26 to 36), while Herod Antipas ruled Galilee, where Jesus grew up and spent most of his ministry. Galilee was a fertile, largely Jewish region of villages and fishing towns around its lake, with Greek-speaking cities nearby.

The Judaism of this period, called Second Temple Judaism because it centered on the temple rebuilt after the exile and greatly enlarged by Herod, was varied. The Pharisees, a lay movement devoted to careful keeping of the law and its traditions, had wide popular influence. The Sadducees were an aristocratic, priestly party connected with the temple. Scribes were experts in the law. Many Jews longed for God to fulfill his promises, drive out the Romans, and restore the kingdom to Israel, and several would-be messiahs and prophets arose in the first century. Matthew's first readers, a generation or more later, likely lived in a mixed community of Jewish and Gentile Christians, in tension with the synagogues around them, working out how faith in Jesus related to the law of Moses and to Israel's hope.
purpose: Matthew wrote to show that Jesus is the Messiah promised in Israel's Scriptures, the son of David and son of Abraham, and that in him the kingdom of heaven has come near. He wrote to teach disciples how to live in that kingdom, gathering Jesus' teaching into blocks that could be learned and passed on, and ending with the command to teach all nations to obey what Jesus commanded (28:20). He also wrote to explain a painful reality for his readers: why many of Israel's leaders rejected their Messiah, and why the Gentiles were now streaming into the people of God. The Gospel reads like a handbook for a community of disciples, a church (Matthew is the only Gospel to use that word, in 16:18 and 18:17), learning to live under the authority of its risen Lord.
story: Matthew stands at the turning point of the Bible's story. The Old Testament ends with Israel back in the land but still waiting: no king on David's throne, the nations still ruling, and Malachi's promise of a messenger and an Elijah still unfulfilled. Around four centuries of Persian, Greek, and Roman rule pass. Matthew picks up exactly there, with a genealogy that runs from Abraham through David and the exile to the Messiah, and with John the Baptist appearing in the wilderness as the promised forerunner. The story Matthew tells, of Jesus' life, death, and resurrection, is the center toward which the Old Testament leads, and it launches the mission to the nations that the book of Acts and the rest of the New Testament go on to describe.
christ:
Matthew presents Jesus through the categories of Israel's hope. He is the son of David, the rightful king, born in David's town and hailed by that title again and again. He is the son of Abraham, through whom the nations will be blessed. He relives Israel's history, coming out of Egypt, passing through the waters, and being tested in the wilderness, and he succeeds where Israel failed. He teaches on a mountain with an authority greater than Moses, saying, you have heard that it was said, but I tell you. He is the servant who bears sickness and suffering, the shepherd of Israel, and the Son of Man who will come in glory.

Above all, he is Immanuel, God with us. The Gospel opens with that name (1:23) and closes with the risen Jesus promising to be with his disciples always, to the end of the age (28:20). Between those two bookends Matthew shows him receiving worship, forgiving sins, and sharing the one divine name with the Father and the Spirit (28:19). Matthew's Jesus is fully the Messiah of Israel and truly God with his people, and his death is the giving of his life as a ransom for many (20:28) and his blood poured out for the forgiveness of sins (26:28).
reading: Read Matthew as a Gospel: a form of ancient biography, centered on its subject's teaching, deeds, and death, written to call readers to faith and discipleship. It is not a modern chronological biography; Matthew often arranges material by theme, grouping teaching into discourses and miracles into clusters (chapters 8 and 9). Watch for three features. First, the fulfillment formulas, about ten times the narrator says this happened to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet, and the Old Testament passage in its own context usually enriches the connection. Second, the five discourses, each ending with a phrase like when Jesus had finished saying these things (7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1; 26:1). Third, the Jewish setting: Matthew assumes knowledge of the law, the Pharisees, the temple, and the Sabbath, and uses the reverent phrase kingdom of heaven where Mark and Luke usually say kingdom of God. Compare the parallel accounts in Mark and Luke to see Matthew's emphases. Avoid reading the Gospel's sharp words against the Pharisees and scribes as a condemnation of the Jewish people; Jesus, his disciples, and Matthew himself were Jews, and the conflict is presented as a dispute within Israel about the meaning of Israel's own Scriptures.

structure.title: The birth and childhood of the Messiah
structure.summary: Jesus' genealogy, his conception by the Holy Spirit, the visit of the Magi, the flight to Egypt, and the settling in Nazareth, each tied to Israel's Scriptures.

structure.title: Preparation and the beginning of ministry
structure.summary: John the Baptist prepares the way, Jesus is baptized and tested in the wilderness, and he begins preaching the kingdom and calling disciples in Galilee.

structure.title: First discourse: the Sermon on the Mount
structure.summary: Jesus teaches the life of the kingdom: the Beatitudes, the fulfillment of the law, true piety, trust in the Father, and the call to hear and do his words.

structure.title: Deeds of power and the mission discourse
structure.summary: A cluster of healings and miracles displays Jesus' authority, and he sends out the twelve with instructions for their mission.

structure.title: Growing opposition and the parables of the kingdom
structure.summary: Doubt and rejection mount, and Jesus teaches in parables about the hidden growth of the kingdom.

structure.title: Who is Jesus? The confession and the community
structure.summary: Feedings, the walk on the water, Peter's confession that Jesus is the Christ, the first predictions of his death, the transfiguration, and teaching on life together in the church.

structure.title: To Jerusalem, conflict, and the end of the age
structure.summary: Jesus travels to Jerusalem, enters as king, clears the temple, debates the leaders, pronounces woes, and teaches about the temple's fall and his return.

structure.title: Death and resurrection
structure.summary: The Last Supper, arrest, trials, crucifixion, and burial, followed by the empty tomb and the risen Jesus commissioning his disciples to make disciples of all nations.

themes.title: Fulfillment
themes.body: Matthew sees Jesus as the goal of Israel's Scriptures. The fulfillment formulas, the genealogy, the patterns that echo Moses and the exodus, and Jesus' own claim that he came not to abolish the Law and the Prophets but to fulfill them (5:17) all present the story of Jesus as the completion of the story of Israel.

themes.title: The kingdom of heaven
themes.body: The central message of John and Jesus is that the kingdom of heaven is near. The phrase means God's reign, arriving in Jesus' own person and work. It is present in his healings and teaching, hidden and growing like a mustard seed, and yet to come in fullness when the Son of Man returns.

themes.title: Discipleship and righteousness
themes.body: Matthew is concerned with what it means to follow Jesus. Disciples are called to a righteousness that exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, not by adding rules but by a heart transformed toward God and neighbor, shown in mercy, forgiveness, humility, and doing the Father's will.

themes.title: Jesus as teacher with authority
themes.body: Matthew gathers Jesus' teaching into five great discourses and repeatedly stresses his authority. He interprets the law, forgives sins, and at the end claims all authority in heaven and on earth (28:18). Many readers have seen in the five discourses a deliberate echo of the five books of Moses.

themes.title: Israel and the nations
themes.body: Jesus is sent first to the lost sheep of Israel (10:6; 15:24), yet Gentiles appear throughout: women in the genealogy, the Magi, a Roman centurion, a Canaanite woman. The Gospel ends with the command to make disciples of all nations, fulfilling the promise to Abraham.

keyChapters.why: The genealogy and the virgin birth introduce Jesus as son of David, son of Abraham, and Immanuel, God with us.
The Beatitudes and Jesus' teaching on fulfilling the law open the Sermon on the Mount, among the most influential moral teaching in history.
The Lord's Prayer and Jesus' teaching on secret piety, treasure, and worry show the inner life of the kingdom.
The parables of the kingdom show how God's reign comes quietly, meets mixed responses, and grows toward a final harvest.
Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ, Jesus speaks of building his church, and he begins to teach that he must suffer, die, and rise.
The Last Supper and Gethsemane show Jesus giving his body and blood for the forgiveness of sins and submitting to his Father's will.
The resurrection and the Great Commission complete the Gospel, with the risen Jesus claiming all authority and promising to be with his disciples always.
